terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to make callout records, searches and grid references and print them.

tasks.title: A callout record
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `callout_records.py`, write a dataclass called `Callout` with three fields, in this order: `date` and `hill`, both text, and `hours`, a whole number. The task asks for `@dataclass`.

Check makes callouts of its own, with values in order and by name, and looks at whether `Callout` is a dataclass, at its fields, at its repr, and at whether two callouts with the same values are equal and two with different hours are not.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on @dataclass.
Put @dataclass on the line above the class line.
Write the three fields, each a name, a colon and a type, in the order the task gives.
Make a callout and print it under the main guard.
hints: A dataclass writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from its fields, so the class needs no def at all.
A field is a name, a colon and a type: `str` for text, `int` for a whole number. A name with `=` and no type is not a field.
The shape is `@dataclass`, then `class Callout:`, then `date: str`, `hill: str` and `hours: int`, each moved in under it.

videos.title: What a dataclass writes for you

tasks.title: A search and its teams
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a dataclass called `Search` with three fields, in this order: `area`, text; `teams`, a list of call signs, a new empty list for each search made without one; and `hours`, a whole number, 0 for a search made without it.

Check makes searches of its own, with only an area and with all three values, adds a team to one search, and looks at whether another search gets it too. It also reads the repr and whether `Search` is a dataclass.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on defaults, and the list trap.
Write the dataclass with area first, as in Task 1.
Give teams a new list for each search with field and default_factory.
Give hours a default of 0, make two searches under the main guard, and add a team to one.
hints: Python refuses a list written straight in as the default of a field, because every search would share that one list.
The dataclasses module's `field` can give a field a maker instead of a value: the kind of value, without round brackets, which the dataclass calls for each new search.
The shape is `@dataclass`, `class Search:`, then `area: str`, `teams: list = field(default_factory=list)` and `hours: int = 0`.

tasks.title: A grid reference that stays put
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write a dataclass called `GridRef` with two fields, `easting` and `northing`, both whole numbers. A `GridRef` cannot be changed once it is made: the task asks for `frozen=True`. Give it a method `moved(east, north)` that gives back a new `GridRef` that many metres east and north of this one. A negative number moves west or south.

Check makes grid references of its own, tries to change one and expects the error a frozen dataclass gives, then calls `moved` and looks at the new grid reference and at whether the old one is as it was.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on a record that stays put.
Write the dataclass with its two fields, and frozen=True in the round brackets of @dataclass.
Write moved inside it, lined up with the fields, giving back a new GridRef.
Make the base and a grid reference moved from it under the main guard, and try to change the base.
hints: A frozen dataclass cannot be changed, not even by its own methods, so moved cannot add to `self.easting`.
Make the new grid reference from this one's values with the distances added. A class can be called inside its own methods, as anywhere else.
The shape is `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, `class GridRef:`, `easting: int`, `northing: int`, then `def moved(self, east, north):` with `return GridRef(self.easting + east, self.northing + north)`.
